scenes.heading: Molecular shape
scenes.sub: Why is water bent but carbon dioxide straight?
scenes.say: A molecule's 3D shape decides whether it's polar, what it dissolves in, and even whether a medicine fits its receptor. VSEPR theory predicts shape from one simple idea: electron domains push as far apart as possible.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A group photo where some friends are invisible but still take up space
scenes.science: Lone pairs shape the molecule but aren't named in the shape
scenes.breaks: lone pairs aren't hidden atoms. They're electron density on the central atom, and they take up MORE room than a bonding pair.
scenes.say: Picture a group photo where some friends are invisible. They still take up space, but the photo only shows the visible people. Lone pairs are the invisible friends. The electron domain geometry includes everyone, but the shape you name shows only the atoms. So ammonia has tetrahedral domains but a trigonal pyramidal shape.

scenes.heading: The VSEPR method
steps: Count domains on the central atom
Name the shape from the atoms
scenes.say: Here's the routine. Draw the Lewis structure. Count domains on the central atom, remembering a multiple bond counts as one. Write the A X E label. Find the electron domain geometry, then name the shape from where the atoms sit.

scenes.heading: Lone pairs are invisible but bossy
points: 6 domains: a 2nd lone pair goes opposite
scenes.say: Lone pairs are like a tram passenger with a huge backpack. They take up more room and squeeze the bonds together, so the angle drops from one hundred and nine point five in methane to one hundred and four point five in water. With five domains, lone pairs go around the waist. With six, a second lone pair sits opposite the first.
scenes.caption: Lone pairs are like a tram passenger with a huge backpack. They take up more room and squeeze the bonds together, so the angle drops from 109.5° in CH₄ to 104.5° in H₂O. With five domains, lone pairs go around the waist. With six, a second lone pair sits opposite the first.

scenes.heading: Worked example: XeF₄
scenes.question: Predict the shape and polarity of XeF₄.
lines: 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs on Xe = 6 domains
AX₄E₂: lone pairs opposite each other
scenes.say: Xenon tetrafluoride has thirty-six valence electrons. That leaves two lone pairs on xenon, so six domains. The lone pairs sit opposite each other, giving a square planar shape. The four bond dipoles point to the corners of a square and cancel, so it's non-polar.

scenes.heading: Polar bonds vs polar molecule
scenes.say: Polar bonds don't always make a polar molecule. Carbon dioxide has polar bonds, but it's linear, so the dipoles cancel. Water is bent, so its dipoles add up. Swap just one atom, like in chloromethane, and a symmetric molecule becomes polar.

points: Domains spread out to minimise repulsion
Polarity = polar bonds + shape that doesn't cancel
scenes.say: Quick recap. Domains spread out to minimise repulsion. Lone pairs squeeze angles but aren't in the shape's name. And polarity needs polar bonds plus a shape where the dipoles don't cancel. Now try the practice questions!
